newsitem.title: UK: LME copper marches higher, Escondida workers vote.
newsitem.headline: LME copper marches higher, Escondida workers vote.

text.p: Copper pushed higher on Wednesday afternoon in lively London Metal Exchange trading as spreads inflated further, but momentum was slower after Tuesday's impressive climb.
Late news that strikers at the world's biggest copper mine in Chile may continue their action appeared to give the market a fillip in after-hours business.
The other metals, however, went their own way, as aluminium hovered above $1,600 per tonne, nickel and zinc added to previous gains, and lead and tin ended soggy, eking out small losses.
Three months copper struggled above $2,350 in morning trading, but after the U.S. market opened prices jumped to a peak of $2,373 and spreads widened again.
Light trade buying was seen and funds which had gone short during the recent correction were covering, traders said.
The benchmark cash/threes spread was bid up to a $160 backwardation by the close, up from $100 on Tuesday evening and around $30 most of last week.
The premium of cash over May was bid at $80 shortly before the close. It has flipped from being at a slight discount last week.

The last major bout of tightness was in late January when the backwardation zoomed out to $300. This was about three months ago and some of the current tightness could be from players who rolled over short positions, some traders said.
The current run up in prices was sparked by a combination of factors and is likely to continue at least in the short-term, analysts said.
"The market is re-focusing on the fundamentals, which are tight," said analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff.
The 1,025-tonne fall in LME stocks on Wednesday brought total inventories below 150,000 tonnes to 149,100 tonnes.
Also underpinning the firm market has been concerns over supply, including a strike at the world's largest copper mine in Chile.

Striking workers at the Escondida mine were likely to vote to continue the stoppage despite a recommendation to go back to work, their trade union leader said on Tuesday afternoon after official business ended.
Three months finished the afternoon kerb up $19 at $2,367, but made further gains in inter-office activity being indicated at $2,282/86 at 1645 GMT.
About 17 percent of the 2,000-strong workforce have walked off their jobs but the firm says operations continue at 85 percent of normal levels.
Also supporting the market are labour talks later this week at Phelps Dodge's Chino mine and a maintenance shutdown at the Kennecott smelter in Utah.
Aluminium held above the psychological $1,600 level after stocks fell by 5,225 tonnes, but had trouble making more progress and stalled at $1,610.
This left it locked between the 100-day moving average on the downside at $1,598 and 30-day moving average on the upside at $1,615.
The market may need to consolidate before gathering steam for an attack at $1,620/25 resistance, analysts said.
Prices ended up $8.50 at $1,601.50.
Nickel got a shot in the arm during the afternoon session, marching to a peak of $7,520, matching the April 10 high at the top of its recent range. It eased back to close $50 higher at $7,475.
The close brings the market above the 100-day moving average at $7,408.
Zinc also looked positive, breaching the 30-day moving average of $1,273 to close $19 firmer at $1,283.
But tin and lead were little inspired by the heated action elsewhere and ended in the negative column.
When tin failed to match Tuesday's $5,840 peak, it eased back to a $30 loss at $5,810.
Lead also made little headway against resistance from $640 to $645 and finished $3 weaker at $639.
Alloy was little traded, but marked up sharply to $1,490/94 from $1,462.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom ++44 171 542-8065
